1260.bp: Phones and watches run small AI language models, and different models work better for different people and tasks. You need to pick which one to use without slowing down or draining battery, and users want to understand why a particular model got recommended.
1260.wh: The fundamental problem is that no single small model is best for everyone. Some models handle genre preferences well, others excel at how-to instructions, but each person's needs are different. Picking the right one requires knowing what kind of person you're talking to and what they're trying to do, which is hard to formalize and explain.

PEARL maps each person's profile (their preferences and behavior patterns) and each model's strengths into a shared mathematical space where similarities become visible. It finds shared underlying patterns (like 'genre sensitivity' or 'instruction-following') and uses those to match people to models. Then it translates the decision back into plain language.
1260.ww: By representing both people and models in the same space with aligned dimensions, you can directly see which people match which models. The key is that these matching dimensions are interpretable (you can read them back as 'likes genre fiction' or 'handles procedures well'), so the system can explain its choices rather than just making them.
1260.po: On real dialogue data, the system picks models that score about 2.23 points better on conversation quality than picking one model for everyone, and it explains every choice. When you hide the top matching pattern, recommendations flip for 60% of people, showing that the system is actually using meaningful, interpretable signals.

1261.bp: Search engines now show AI-written summaries instead of just links, and people read these summaries as if they're reliable. But if the summary is wrong, a user might follow bad advice or make a wrong decision, and they may never know.
1261.wh: A well-written summary with citations looks credible even when it's wrong. The visual design—clean formatting, cited sources—creates false confidence. The real problem is that mistakes hide in three ways: the summary itself is wrong, the cited sources don't actually support what was claimed, or the citations contradict each other.
1261.ap: Researchers took real search queries and compared Google's AI summaries to the actual sources the search engine cited. They checked whether the summary statement was factually correct, whether the cited passages truly support it, and whether different citations agree with each other.
1261.ww: By measuring the gap between what a summary appears to claim and what its sources actually say, you expose a hidden reliability problem. Visual polish and citations create trust that isn't earned by the underlying evidence, so users need to see where the real cracks are.
1261.po: One in three summaries are factually wrong, and among those errors, most happen even when the right sources were right there to cite. Citations also contradict each other one time in three, and the problem gets worse as more sources are piled on. This reveals a systemic risk that today's search designs hide from users.

1262.bp: When you search for documents by similarity, AI systems store dense mathematical representations of each doc—vectors of hundreds of numbers. These files get huge fast, so you have to shrink the vectors to save disk space and search speed. But shrinking risks losing information.
1262.wh: Standard shrinking methods have opposite flaws. One method (PCA) keeps the strongest patterns but wastes capacity in weaker directions. The other (whitening) treats all directions equally but amplifies noise in the weak directions, where signal is already thin. You can't win by picking one extreme.
1262.ap: The method treats shrinking as a tuning problem: scale each direction's importance by a power of itself, with bigger numbers getting scaled more aggressively. Instead of picking a fixed scale for all vectors and dimensions, the system computes the best per-dimension scale automatically from the data's natural noise profile, without needing to label data or try many settings.
1262.ww: Noise in weak directions has a distinctive fingerprint you can measure from the data alone. By tuning how much you preserve each direction based on its local signal-to-noise ratio, you keep the good stuff and discard the noise automatically, all without trial-and-error or labeled examples.
1262.po: The method gets nearly the same quality as if you had tuned the scaling by hand (testing thousands of values), but it's fully automatic, doesn't need labeled data, and works across different search tasks and models without retraining.

1263.bp: Search engines sometimes try to guess better queries by looking at what came back—if you search for 'apple', maybe you meant 'apple computer', so they re-query. This can help, but sometimes it makes things worse. You need to know which queries it actually helps.
1263.wh: Past methods use offline metrics to guess whether re-querying will help, but those metrics measure how good the results look, not how good they feel to a real person typing at a keyboard. A person's true judgment (did this search actually help me?) is hidden unless you ask them.
1263.ap: Researchers showed real people searches side-by-side using a grid layout, displaying some results with the original query and some with the re-queried version, randomizing positions to avoid position bias. They then used a method (Team Draft Interleaving) that watches which results people click to infer their actual preference, without interrupting the natural search flow.
1263.ww: By watching real people interacting with real searches instead of guessing from metrics, you learn what actually matters to them. Some queries people prefer not to re-query on (better to just refine the original), and avoiding harm there is more valuable than amplifying help elsewhere.
1263.po: When tested this way, only one in five queries improved, one in four got worse, and the gap is huge: skipping harmful re-queries gave 68% improvement whereas amplifying helpful ones gave only 37%. This flips the common assumption that more re-querying is always better.

1264.bp: When people search conversationally ('show me Italian restaurants near museums'), the system needs to guess what category of thing they're after ('restaurant', 'museum', 'cuisine'). Grouping conversations into the right category helps the system answer better.
1264.wh: Traditional clustering methods ask you to guess how many categories exist, and they assign each conversation to exactly one category. But a conversation about Italian restaurants near museums could belong partly to food and partly to sightseeing. Also, starting by picking a category count is arbitrary and fragile.
1264.ap: Instead of one label per conversation, generate many possible labels (using an AI system to propose different interpretations), collect all these labels, and treat them as a cloud of possibilities. Then build a representation by combining where the conversation's core meaning sits with where the average of all its possible labels sits. Finally, group conversations that share overlapping label clouds together.
1264.ww: By allowing multiple interpretations per conversation and letting the grouping emerge from shared interpretations (rather than forcing one-to-one assignment), you capture the fuzzy nature of what people are searching for. The system doesn't need you to guess the category count upfront.
1264.po: The method beats recent systems on four standard benchmarks without asking for a cluster count, and it avoids the instability of tuning toward a single label per query.

1265.bp: AI systems can now ask questions, look up facts, think through answers, then ask new questions—doing research-like work automatically. But they often waste time re-fetching information they already found or overthinking questions they've solved.
1265.wh: As these systems get smarter and more capable, they don't get more efficient—they actually spend more resources doing redundant work. You can spot the problem (fetched this article three times? thinking for fifty steps on a two-step question?), but you can't easily fix it without breaking what makes them work.
1265.ap: Researchers measured overthinking and over-retrieval in different ways: statistics like how many times a document was fetched, and also AI-based judgment of whether reasoning steps seemed productive or circular. They then fed these signals back as explicit rewards, guiding the system's future choices toward being more focused.
1265.ww: By making inefficiency visible and quantifiable, you can train systems to notice when they're stuck in loops or fetching things redundantly. Larger models are already somewhat better at avoiding these problems, but even they can be nudged toward efficiency by showing them exactly where they're wasting effort.
1265.po: The framework reveals that model size helps reduce both behaviors, but by different amounts, and that explicit feedback based on these measurements can steer a system toward faster, leaner research-like work without sacrificing accuracy.

1266.bp: When you search for images and text together (like finding 'a golden retriever sleeping on a couch' in a photo collection), the system should understand that 'dog' and 'golden retriever' are related—they're at different levels of detail. Respecting this structure makes search better.
1266.wh: Current search systems treat all concepts as if they're equally different from each other: 'dog' and 'car' seem equally unrelated as 'dog' and 'golden retriever'. But humans know these are different levels of specificity. Regular geometric math doesn't capture hierarchy well—you need special math that treats containment differently.
1266.ap: The method adapts already-trained cross-modal systems (like CLIP) by adding a special mathematical layer (hyperbolic geometry) only at the point where image and text similarities are compared, while keeping the core model in ordinary math. This lets you fine-tune only a small part (LoRA) without retraining the whole thing.
1266.ww: Hyperbolic geometry naturally captures hierarchies (general concepts contain specific ones, the way 'dog' contains 'golden retriever'). By layering this hierarchy math only at similarity computation, you get hierarchy awareness without costly retraining or breaking what the original model learned.
1266.po: The system matches standard pre-trained models on speed and general performance, but improves recall by 70-90% when hierarchy matters, and adds 2-6% on top of standard models. All of this works with no costly retraining.

1267.bp: People with speech disabilities or unclear thoughts struggle to type a search query. If you could read brain activity directly to understand what they're looking for, you could help them find information without typing. But which brain patterns work best?
1267.wh: Recent work claims that listening to audio produces better brain patterns for this task than watching text, but those studies used different datasets, different vocabulary, and different corpus sizes. You can't tell if audio is genuinely better or if the setup just favored audio.
1267.ap: Researchers took two brain-imaging datasets (one from auditory studies, one from visual), balanced them for vocabulary overlap and sample sizes, and trained identical neural systems on both. They mapped brain activity to document meanings using contrastive learning—the same method for both modalities, only the sensory input changed.
1267.ww: By controlling the experimental setup (same models, same vocabulary, same corpus), you can separate real differences in how brains process audio versus text from artifacts of the experimental design. Different modalities might have genuinely different strengths.
1267.po: Under equal conditions, audio-based brain activity retrieves more documents overall (recall 74-140% better), while visual-based brain activity is more precise (finding the exact right document first is 100% better). This shows both have complementary strengths that could both be useful in a real system.

1268.bp: Recommendation systems learn what users like from their history, but when a new item arrives, there's no history yet. You need to guess whether someone will like it based only on its description or images. This is the 'cold-start' problem.
1268.wh: Existing methods try to mix the new item's descriptions into the learned patterns from user history, but users' patterns and item features live in different mathematical worlds—there's a mismatch that no amount of mixing fully heals. Some users might prefer detailed descriptions while others only care about images.
1268.ap: Instead of mixing user history with item features, treat recommendation as learning item-to-item similarity purely from content (text, images). Use a softer version of standard training that explicitly zeros out gradients for negative examples that don't teach anything, letting the system focus on meaningful contrasts. Knowledge from successful old items is transferred to new ones.
1268.ww: By ignoring the mismatch between user history and item features, and instead learning pure item similarity from content alone, you avoid the alignment problem. Zeroing gradients on uninformative negatives means the system focuses training energy on comparisons that matter, making efficient use of limited data.
1268.po: The method beats existing cold-start approaches, and as a bonus, it naturally treats all items fairly—older items with lots of user history can't dominate recommendations just by having more training examples.

1269.bp: When you search for something and click on promising results, the system can learn from those clicks to improve future searches. It's called relevance feedback. But sometimes a clicked document actually steers the system the wrong way, producing worse results.
1269.wh: Past work looked only at single feedback documents, but in practice you'll click on multiple results. Sometimes a bad document combines with good ones to cause problems, and sometimes a bad document alone is bad, but with others becomes useful. These interactions are hidden.
1269.ap: Researchers tested feedback across multiple datasets and multiple retrieval methods (lexical and neural). They measured how sets of feedback documents combined: whether a 'poison pill' (harmful document) stayed harmful when combined with others, and whether combinations that worked well individually worked together.
1269.ww: By looking at combinations rather than single documents, you discover that feedback works as a system—a document's effect depends on what other documents you feedback on. Neural methods are more effective on average but also more brittle, suggesting they're learning more complex, context-dependent patterns.
1269.po: The findings show that neural feedback is both more powerful and more fragile than lexical feedback, and that document interactions matter: a poison pill alone can become helpful in the right combination, and vice versa.

1270.bp: When comparing ranking algorithms, you need a score that says 'these results are better' or 'these are worse'. Today's standard metric heavily weights the top few results and lightly weights the bottom. But you might want different trade-offs for different applications.
1270.wh: Existing rank-biased scoring uses one parameter that controls how fast the weight decays down the ranking. One parameter is rigid—it locks you into one trade-off. Different experiments might need different balances (some care deeply about top-1 result, others care about top-10).
1270.ap: The paper shows that adding a second mathematical parameter gives you more flexibility in weighting. Different mathematical functions (power laws, geometric decay) can all be tuned with two parameters instead of one, letting you shape exactly how much each position matters.
1270.ww: A second parameter lets you independently control both the overall weight decay shape and the strength of that decay. This means you can measure rankings in a way that fits what your application actually needs, rather than forcing every experiment into the same mold.
1270.po: The result is a measurement toolbox that suits more real-world scenarios than existing methods, letting experimenters choose trade-offs explicitly rather than living with default assumptions about what matters in a ranking.

1271.bp: When you ask 'What invention most changed transportation?' the answer isn't directly in any single sentence—you have to connect ideas ('the automobile', 'speed', 'commerce'). AI systems need to reason through multiple pieces of evidence, not just copy them.
1271.wh: Most search-augmented systems grab passages with the highest similarity scores, but similarity doesn't measure whether a passage helps narrow down to the right answer. A passage might be on-topic but misleading, or correct but useless for reasoning.
1271.ap: Researchers measured 'convergence'—how much each sentence eliminates wrong answers and points toward the right one. They built passages using high-convergence sentences and tested whether AI systems reason better with them, compared to passages selected by standard similarity.
1271.ww: Convergence captures something beyond topicality: how much a piece of evidence actually constrains the answer space. By selecting sentences that actively steer toward the right answer rather than just matching the question, you give the AI better raw material for multi-step reasoning.
1271.po: Passages built from high-convergence sentences lead to substantially better reasoning accuracy than similarity-selected passages, and ordering by convergence helps even more, suggesting AI systems pay attention to early signals when reasoning.

1272.bp: Language models seem biased toward well-known people and places, naming them more often and rating them as more important. Is this bias a problem with the model itself, or is the model just learning what was actually common in real-world text?
1272.wh: Most language models' training data is secret, so you can't tell whether a model's preference for famous things reflects real-world importance or statistical accident. Even if you think popularity bias is a problem, you can't diagnose it without data.
1272.ap: Researchers used the open OLMo model and its fully public training corpus (7.4 trillion tokens) to count exactly how often each person, place, and organization appeared. They then compared those exposure counts to what the model claims about importance.
1272.ww: By having the training data fully visible, you can separate real exposure from model preference. If the model mostly prefers things that appeared more often in training, it's not behaving bizarrely—it's learning the statistical patterns it sees.
1272.po: Model preferences align much more closely with pretraining exposure than with objective measures like Wikipedia popularity. This is especially true for larger models and for lesser-known entities. The finding suggests popularity bias in language models is primarily learned from training data patterns, not a model flaw.

1273.bp: When answering questions that require chaining facts together ('Who directed the movie where actor X met actor Y?'), search has to find evidence across multiple documents. But standard similarity math collapses structure—it forgets that one document has to connect to another.
1273.wh: Graph-based search tries to preserve these connection patterns, but standard math for measuring similarity treats 'close' and 'far' as simple distances, which doesn't capture containment (one fact lives within a larger structure). You get 'semantically relevant but structurally useless' results ranking high.
1273.ap: A reranking module compares the structure of the query and candidate evidence using special geometry (hyperbolic space, which naturally represents hierarchies), alongside semantic similarity. It adapts the balance between structure and semantics based on whether the query itself demands multi-hop reasoning.
1273.ww: Hierarchical math (hyperbolic geometry) naturally captures how facts nest inside larger contexts. By reranking to favor structurally sound chains (even if semantically similar items exist), you get evidence that actually chains together for multi-hop reasoning.
1273.po: The method improves results on four reasoning benchmarks, with the biggest gains when hierarchical reasoning is demanded, and stays robust when reasoning is flatter. It works as a plug-in layer with no model retraining.

1274.bp: Language models trained on everything know almost everything, but each user wants recommendations tailored to them. You need to adapt the model to each person without retraining, and you need it to understand both user history (behavior) and content descriptions (semantics).
1274.wh: Existing methods mix behavioral and semantic signals either early (injecting user patterns into token space, but the spaces are misaligned) or late (learning two separate adaptations and combining them, but they may disagree). Both approaches leave structural gaps.
1274.ap: The system adds personalized low-rank changes (LoRA) to the language model's core weights in a way that creates two different versions at once: one tuned to behavioral patterns, one to semantic meaning. An adaptive fusion module learns how to blend these two views into a single user preference per person.
1274.ww: By treating the same model weights as a shared space where two independent personalized adaptations can coexist with minimal conflict, you avoid the mismatch between behavioral and semantic signals. Fusion happens at the output level where both views are ready, not during processing.
1274.po: The system beats state-of-the-art approaches on four test datasets, and A/B testing in real-world use showed significant gains in user engagement. The dual-view approach captures both what users do and what items mean.
